Which signal detection method finds adverse drug reactions best, and earliest?

A benchmark of PRR, ROR, BCPNN and EBGM on 12 years of FDA FAERS data

Author

Joan Fortunet

Published

November 15, 2026

Summary

Pharmacovigilance teams screen millions of spontaneous reports for signals: drug–reaction pairs reported more often than expected. Four statistical methods dominate in practice: the proportional reporting ratio (PRR), the reporting odds ratio (ROR), the Bayesian confidence propagation neural network (BCPNN, WHO) and the multi-item gamma Poisson shrinker (MGPS/EBGM, FDA). This project implements all four from scratch and compares them on the FDA Adverse Event Reporting System (FAERS), 2014 Q3 – 2026 Q2, against two references built from FDA drug labels.

Main findings

  • With many reports, the four methods agree (Jaccard 0.81–0.87 between PRR, ROR and BCPNN). They differ where it matters most, on rare pairs: 44 % of all drug–reaction pairs have a single report, and the Bayesian methods shrink them.
  • Against current labels, the raw number of reports ranks known reactions better than any disproportionality method, because labels list many common, non-specific reactions. On serious, typically drug-induced events all four methods perform the same (AUC ≈ 0.74).
  • Disproportionality often sees reactions years before the FDA adds them to the label: by the date of the label change, ROR had flagged 55 % of them, BCPNN 52 %, PRR 48 % and EBGM 36 %.
  • There is a clear speed–specificity trade-off: EBGM raises the fewest false alarms but flags reactions a median of 3–6 months later than BCPNN or PRR. BCPNN gives the best balance.
  • A gradient boosting model that combines the four scores with the case mix (seriousness, reporter type, dynamics) clearly outperforms every single method as a triage score (average precision 0.36 vs 0.08).
  • Case studies show what statistics cannot do alone: the ranitidine “cancer” signal is an artefact of litigation-driven reporting.

1. Data

The pipeline (Python + DuckDB, all steps tested) keeps the latest version of each case as recommended by the FDA, removes deleted cases, normalises drug names (salts, biosimilar suffixes, combination order) and excludes preferred terms that are not adverse reactions (medication errors, off-label use, lack of efficacy, product complaints, exposures; 15 % of reaction rows).

Reports come mostly from consumers (44 %) and from the US (69 %); age is missing in 43 % of cases. The drug–reaction table is extremely sparse:

2. Methods

Method Estimate Signal when
PRR Proportional reporting ratio (95 % CI) a ≥ 3, PRR ≥ 2, χ² ≥ 4 (Evans et al., 2001)
ROR Reporting odds ratio (95 % CI) a ≥ 3 and lower bound > 1
BCPNN Information component with shrinkage IC025 > 0 (Norén et al., 2006, 2013)
MGPS Empirical Bayes geometric mean, two-gamma prior EB05 ≥ 2 (DuMouchel, 1999)

The EBGM implementation was validated against a posterior computed by direct numerical integration, and its prior fit against simulated data.

3. Evaluation design

Reference 1 – current labels. For the 300 most reported drugs, the current FDA label was taken from openFDA. A pair is positive if its reaction appears in the boxed warning, contraindications, warnings and precautions or adverse reactions; negative if it does not appear anywhere in the label (285 drugs, 982 k pairs, 3.2 % positive).

Reference 2 – dated label changes. The FDA Safety-related Labeling Changes database lists every safety change since 2016 with the text added. A reaction mentioned in an addition gets the date of the change (4,785 reactions, 261 drugs). The database is then replayed quarter by quarter, using only cases received by each date, to find when each method first flagged each reaction.

4. Results

Ranking known reactions

Machine learning

The most important feature is how often a reaction is reported overall: part of the gain comes from learning which kinds of reactions end up on labels. The model is best seen as a triage score on top of the statistical signal.

6. Limitations

  • Spontaneous reports cannot give incidence or prove causality, and are affected by notoriety bias, stimulated reporting and confounding by indication.
  • Both references rely on matching MedDRA preferred terms to label text: synonyms are missed (for example suicidal thoughts vs suicidal ideation), so some true reactions count as negatives.
  • A label change marks when the FDA acted, not when a reaction became known.
  • The replay uses the latest version of each case, which may contain information that was not available at the time.
  • Only primary suspect drugs and drugs with an available label were analysed.

Reproducibility

All code, tests and reference files are in github.com/joanfortunet/faers-signal-benchmark: make data builds the warehouse, make reference and make benchmark run the evaluation, and make app opens the interactive signal explorer.
